title: Attending to Others When What You Crave Is Attention
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In this installment of his depressurization series, Stuart addresses the paradox of craving attention in an attention-starved world: the solution, he argues, is to give attention rather than seek it. Drawing on Arthur Brooks's Atlantic piece on fame and happiness, he reinterprets the childhood fixation on fame as really being about a more universal human need to be seen, known, and appreciated, and concludes the fastest way to meet that need in yourself is to meet it in someone else. He offers three school-based practices — verbally thanking a colleague for something admirable spotted in an email, scanning your class roster each morning for something to notice and affirm in a student, and reflecting back what someone says in conversation to signal genuine listening — plus parallel versions for use at home. He is careful to frame these as soul-care practices done freely rather than manipulative tactics for extracting reciprocal attention, warning that entering into them transactionally will undermine their effect.
points: Stuart's central move reframes attention-craving as solvable through a counter-intuitive mechanism: give the specific thing you're craving (being noticed, heard, valued) to someone else rather than seeking it directly.

He reinterprets Brooks's fame statistics (children wanting to be YouTubers, 92% of adults linking success to being 'well-known') as evidence of a deeper, more universal craving for attention and appreciation, not fame itself.

The 'scanning the roster for a smile' practice explicitly merges two existing systems — tracking moments of genuine connection and this depressurization exercise — so the technique adds no separate workload.

He draws a sharp line against using these practices instrumentally, warning that doing them to make other people reciprocate attention will both fail and defeat the purpose; they only work when done 'freely and gladly.'
quotes: Ours is, ironically, an attention-starved world. With more things than ever competing for our attention, the folks in our lives tend to miss out.
But this is what I took away: what we want isn't fame, but to be seen, known, appreciated. We want the loving attention of other people. Especially people we care about.

I find this in-person action a lot better at depressurizing my soul than sending a "Reply All" or "Reply" with the same affirmation. Emails add pressure to the social sphere; genuine, in-person affirmations depressurize it.

I'm been thinking lately of getting a tattoo written backwards on my forehead that says, "LISTEN. REFLECT. SERVE." These are things that don't come naturally to me, and my worst seasons relationally are the ones in which I neglect them.

The most critical thing with all of these is that you are not doing them to get any desired action from other people. You are doing them because you've got a soul that needs relief and because they're human beings wrought with a dumbfounding weight of dignity.

Before you know it, you'll see: folks will start attending to you, and you won't be an attention-starved creature when they do because your need for attention will have diminished via giving it to others.
